title: Spices and Perfume
lead: Spices and perfumed oils came to Israel by caravan and ship from Arabia, India and farther east. They were used in worship (the holy anointing oil, Exodus 30:22–33), in burial (John 19:39), at feasts and weddings (Psalm 45:8; Esther 2:12), and in love (Proverbs 7:17; Song of Songs). The Song of Songs uses them more than any other book: nard, myrrh, henna, saffron, calamus, cinnamon, aloes, frankincense and 'spices'.

sections.h: Perfume in worship and in burial
sections.b: The holy anointing oil was made of liquid myrrh, cinnamon, calamus and cassia in olive oil (Exodus 30:22–25). Nicodemus brought myrrh and aloes to Jesus' burial (John 19:39), and the women went to the tomb with spices (Mark 16:1). Mary of Bethany poured a pound of pure nard on Jesus' feet (John 12:3).

sections.h: Perfume in royal and private life
sections.b: Esther prepared for the king with a year of myrrh and perfumes (Esther 2:12). Psalm 45:8 says the king's robes smell of myrrh, aloes and cassia. The queen of Sheba brought spices to Solomon (1 Kings 10:2, 10). In Proverbs 7:17 the foreign woman perfumes her bed with myrrh, aloes and cinnamon. The Song uses the same scents for the lovers' own bed and garden, so that the perfumes are not wicked in themselves, only in the use made of them.
